title: Write a query to find duplicate customer emails (`GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`), and explain why the application-level `if (!emailExists) insert` check is NOT enough under concurrency and must be backed by a DB `UNIQUE` constraint (the app validates, the database enforces).
shortTitle: Duplicate Customer Emails and Why App-Level Checks Need a DB UNIQUE Constraint

s1_definition.profdef: Finding duplicate emails groups by a normalized email and keeps groups with a count above one. The deeper point is that an application-level "check-then-insert" (`if (!emailExists) insert`) is a race condition: between the check and the insert, another thread or node can insert the same email, so both succeed. Only a database `UNIQUE` constraint, which the engine enforces atomically at write time, guarantees no duplicates. The app validates for a friendly message; the database enforces for correctness.
s1_definition.analogy: Two people walk up to two different counters at the National Bank of India at the exact same second, both wanting to register the email rajesh@x.com. Each teller checks "is this email taken?" — both see "no" because neither registration is saved yet — and both say "go ahead." Now the email exists twice. The only fix is a rule stamped on the ledger itself that physically refuses a second identical email, no matter how many tellers are working. That ledger rule is the `UNIQUE` constraint.
s1_definition.oneliner: `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds dupes, but the app's check-then-insert races under concurrency — only a DB `UNIQUE` constraint truly prevents duplicates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding duplicate emails groups by a normalized email and keeps groups with a count above one. The deeper point is that an application-level "check-then-insert" (`if (!emailExists) insert`) is a race condition: between the check and the insert, another thread or node can insert the same email, so both succeed. Only a database `UNIQUE` constraint, which the engine enforces atomically at write time, guarantees no duplicates. The app validates for a friendly message; the database enforces for correctness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two people walk up to two different counters at the National Bank of India at the exact same second, both wanting to register the email rajesh@x.com. Each teller checks "is this email taken?" — both see "no" because neither registration is saved yet — and both say "go ahead." Now the email exists twice. The only fix is a rule stamped on the ledger itself that physically refuses a second identical email, no matter how many tellers are working. That ledger rule is the `UNIQUE` constraint.

**One line to remember:** `GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` finds dupes, but the app's check-then-insert races under concurrency — only a DB `UNIQUE` constraint truly prevents duplicates.

sections.s2_technical:
The detection query is the standard duplicate pattern, with normalization because emails are case-insensitive in practice:

```sql
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS norm_email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM customers
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

`LOWER(TRIM(email))` folds `Rajesh@X.com` and ` rajesh@x.com ` into the same key so near-duplicates are caught, grouping buckets by that key, and `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` keeps only the repeated ones.

The core teaching point is why this situation arises and how to prevent it. A very common but broken pattern in application code is check-then-act:

```java
if (!customerRepo.existsByEmail(email)) {   // step 1: check
    customerRepo.insert(new Customer(email)); // step 2: insert
}
```

This looks safe for a single thread, but under concurrency it has a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. Imagine two requests arrive simultaneously with the same email. Thread A runs the check and sees the email does not exist. Before A inserts, Thread B also runs the check and also sees it does not exist, because A has not committed yet. Both then insert, and you have two rows with the same email. This is not a rare theoretical case; at scale, with retries and double-clicks, it happens regularly. Raising the database isolation level does not reliably fix it either, because the two transactions are inserting new rows that each other cannot "see," so even SERIALIZABLE may allow it unless there is a constraint or you use explicit locking.

The correct, durable fix is a database `UNIQUE` constraint:

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email UNIQUE (email);
```

The database enforces uniqueness atomically as part of the write. If two concurrent inserts race, the first to commit wins and the second fails with a unique-violation error, which the application catches and turns into a friendly "email already registered" message. The application-level check is still useful — it gives a fast, friendly response in the common non-racing case and avoids an exception on every normal duplicate — but it is an optimization, not the guarantee. The guarantee lives in the database.

Senior-level details: for case-insensitive uniqueness you either store emails already lowercased, or create a functional unique index `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON customers (LOWER(email))`, or use a case-insensitive type like PostgreSQL's `citext`; a plain `UNIQUE(email)` would still allow `A@x.com` and `a@x.com` as distinct. The robust write pattern is "try the insert, catch the unique violation" (optimistic), or use an upsert like `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING`. The principle generalizes far beyond emails: any invariant that must never be violated (unique account numbers, one active loan per customer, non-negative balance) belongs as a database constraint, because the database is the single serialization point that all concurrent clients funnel through. The mantra is: the application validates, the database enforces.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's online registration lets customers sign up with an email. Rajesh double-clicked the submit button on a slow connection, firing two near-simultaneous registration requests with rajesh@x.com. The code used `if (!emailExists) insert`, both requests passed the check before either committed, and two customer rows were created with the same email, which later broke password-reset (two accounts matched one email). The fix had two parts: a detection query to find existing duplicate emails for cleanup, and a `UNIQUE` constraint so it can never recur.

This demonstrates both the duplicate-detection query and the concurrency race. Our mini-project simulates two concurrent threads doing check-then-insert to show the race producing a duplicate, then shows an enforced version that rejects the second insert.

The code will contain: a `CustomerRow`, a `CustomerStore` that simulates a table with and without a unique constraint, a `RegistrationService` with the broken check-then-insert and a safe enforced insert, a `DuplicateFinder` for the detection query, and a `Demo` that runs two threads concurrently to expose the race.

```bash

mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run
java -cp target/email-uniqueness-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.reg.RegistrationApplication

# Expected output (the broken path may occasionally show 2 rows due to the race):
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two concurrent registration requests, both for rajesh@x.com, hitting first the broken store and then the enforced store.

Step 1: In the broken store both threads call `existsByEmail("rajesh@x.com")`. Because neither has inserted yet, both get `false`. This is the fatal moment — the check-then-insert race window.

Step 2: Both threads, believing the email is free, call `insertNoCheck`. Two rows are created with the same email. The data now violates the intended invariant, and the detection query confirms `rajesh@x.com` has a count of two.

Step 3: Against the enforced store the first `registerEnforced` inserts successfully, holding the lock during the atomic insert. The second `registerEnforced` runs the enforced insert, finds the email already present inside the same atomic operation, and throws a unique-violation, which the service catches and turns into a friendly warning.

Step 4: The enforced store always ends with exactly one row for the email, regardless of concurrency, because the database (simulated by the synchronized atomic insert) is the single serialization point.

Step 5: The application prints both outcomes side by side, proving that only the database-enforced version is safe.

```
Oct 25, 2026 16:55:40 WARNING: Rejected duplicate email (friendly message): rajesh@x.com
BROKEN store rows: 2 (expected 1, race made 2)
Duplicates found: {rajesh@x.com=2}
ENFORCED store rows: 1 (always 1)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Two concurrent requests: register rajesh@x.com
    │
    ├─ BROKEN: check-then-insert (no DB constraint)
    │     Thread A: exists? NO ──┐
    │     Thread B: exists? NO ──┤  (both checked before either inserted)
    │     Thread A: INSERT       │
    │     Thread B: INSERT       ▼
    │     → 2 rows (DUPLICATE)  GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT>1 → {rajesh@x.com:2}
    │
    └─ ENFORCED: DB UNIQUE constraint
          Thread A: INSERT → commit ✓
          Thread B: INSERT → UNIQUE violation ✗ → caught → friendly "already registered"
          → 1 row (always)
```

With five service instances, no in-memory check is authoritative — only the single database primary's unique index serializes all concurrent inserts and guarantees correctness.

sections.s6_takeaway:
To find duplicate emails I group by a normalized email and keep groups with a count above one: `SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)), COUNT(*) FROM customers GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, normalizing so case and whitespace variations are caught. But the more important part of this question is why they exist. An application check like `if (!emailExists) insert` is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: under concurrency two requests with the same email both run the existence check before either commits, both see "not present," and both insert, producing a duplicate. Raising the isolation level does not reliably help because each transaction is inserting a new row the other cannot see yet. The only robust fix is a database UNIQUE constraint, because the database is the single serialization point that every concurrent client funnels through, and it enforces uniqueness atomically at write time.

In our National Bank of India registration flow a customer double-clicked submit on a slow connection, two near-simultaneous requests both passed the check-then-insert, and two accounts ended up sharing one email, which later broke password reset. I cleaned up the existing duplicates with the detection query and added a case-insensitive unique index on the lowercased email so it can never recur, and I kept the application-level check only as a friendly-message optimization for the common non-racing case while catching the unique-violation for the race. The principle I always state is that the application validates but the database enforces, and that any invariant that must never be violated — unique account numbers, one active loan per customer, a non-negative balance — belongs as a database constraint. The line I remember is: the app's check-then-insert races, so back every uniqueness rule with a DB UNIQUE constraint.
